verdict.what: method named `apply` across unrelated domains

verdict.what: GLSL uniform declarations required by PixiJS filter shaders
verdict.notes: These are GLSL shader source strings embedded in JS files, not JS code. The three uniforms (outputFrame, inputClamp, uSampler) are mandatory PixiJS filter shader boilerplate — the framework requires them in every filter's fragment shader. They cannot be factored into a JS helper because GLSL has no include/import mechanism at runtime without a custom preprocessor. A string-template preprocessor could theoretically inject them, but that would add build complexity and obscure shader source for zero real benefit, since each file is already minimal and self-contained.

verdict.what: methods named `clear` that reset local state
verdict.notes: All five are unrelated `clear` methods on different classes/closures with different state shapes: PIXI mark destruction, array reset, request map deletion, array truncation, and layer clearing. The name is a common convention for cleanup methods, not shared logic. No factorization opportunity exists.

verdict.what: reading a module setting to return a boolean
verdict.notes: Each `isEnabled` reads a *different* setting key specific to its own feature. They share only the trivial one-liner shape (a single `getModuleSetting` call), not any common logic. A shared helper would require passing the key as an argument, which gives zero reduction in code — every call site would still need a unique key constant. The double-negation in token-ground-shadow.js further signals these are independent implementations. This is coincidental naming, not factorizable duplication.

verdict.what: Standard PIXI filter uniform declarations (inputSize, outputFrame, inputClamp) repeated verbatim in every GLSL shader string
verdict.notes: These are framework-required PIXI.js filter uniforms — boilerplate every PIXI filter shader must declare. Factoring into a shared const string and template-literal-interpolating it into each shader source reduces copy-paste drift if PIXI's required uniforms change, but adds indirection to what developers expect to see inline in shader code. Worth doing only if the filter files already use template literals or a shader-builder pattern; otherwise the cure is marginally worse than the disease.

verdict.what: Standard PixiJS filter uniform declarations (opacity, inputSize, outputFrame) repeated verbatim at the top of every GLSL shader string
verdict.notes: These are framework-required PixiJS uniforms that every filter shader must declare, making them expected boilerplate rather than accidental duplication. Factoring requires each .js file to import the constant and use template-literal interpolation (e.g. `${FILTER_COMMON_UNIFORMS}`) inside its GLSL string, which is a trivial mechanical change across all 12 files and eliminates the risk of one file diverging (e.g. adding mediump to opacity or changing precision). The main caveat is that inline GLSL is already hard to read; string interpolation adds one more layer of indirection. Worth doing if the codebase already uses other shared GLSL string fragments; skip if shaders are otherwise self-contained.

verdict.what: cleanup/teardown logic named `dispose`
verdict.notes: All six instances are structurally different: they clean up different resources (ticker, event listeners, graphics, session bindings, layer state). The shared name `dispose` is a conventional lifecycle method pattern, not duplicated logic. Factoring would require a generic cleanup mechanism that obscures what each site actually tears down, hurting clarity with no real gain. Two of the six are empty stubs. This is a false positive from name-matching.

verdict.what: bilinear value noise: sample 4 hash1 corners and mix(mix()) over fractional coords
verdict.helper: VALUE_NOISE_GLSL (exported string constant containing the full noise(vec2 p) GLSL function)
verdict.notes: These are almost certainly identical value-noise functions embedded as GLSL strings in JS. Extract the full noise() function body into a shared JS string constant and template-interpolate or concatenate it into each shader source. Risk: if any file's surrounding a/b assignments or hash1 signature differs slightly, verify before merging. Otherwise this is textbook dead-simple extraction.

verdict.what: Dialog cancel button object: fixed icon, localized 'cancel' label, callback resolving promise with null
verdict.notes: The only variable is the `resolve` reference from the enclosing Promise, so the helper just takes resolve as a parameter and returns the plain object. All 5 sites are identical. misc-tools.js already hosts one of the sites and is the natural home for small dialog utilities.

verdict.what: all six are local/closure re-render callbacks named `rebuild` in unrelated UI components

verdict.what: identical GLSL hash1+vnoise function pair copy-pasted verbatim into every effect shader string
verdict.helper: VNOISE_GLSL — shared string constant containing hash1 and vnoise GLSL definitions
verdict.notes: These are GLSL source strings embedded in JS files. A shared JS module can export a VNOISE_GLSL template-literal constant; each shader file imports it and interpolates it into its shader source string. Risk is low if shader string assembly is straightforward (simple concatenation or template literal), but needs verification that all 5 shaders build their source the same way. The flagged 3 lines are just a subset of the real duplication — the full hash1+vnoise block (11 lines) is what should be extracted.

verdict.what: panel lifecycle boilerplate: _resetPanel → build DOM → _mount
verdict.notes: All four open() methods implement the same interface contract (reset, build, mount) but the bodies are entirely different domains: bond state management, glossary search/filter, chat log rendering, and status effect management with favorites. The shared bookends (_resetPanel / _mount) are already inherited from a base class and cannot be further factored without collapsing distinct panel logic into an unreadable callback. This is a framework-required shape, not duplicated logic.

verdict.what: convert degrees to radians and write sin/cos components into this.uniforms.dirV
verdict.notes: Identical 3-line idiom across 4 sibling filter files; all operate on the same uniforms.dirV shape. Extract as a standalone function (not a method) so any filter can call it. Watch for cases where the caller may later override dirV[0]/dirV[1] individually — verify no such code follows the snippet before replacing.

verdict.what: initializing the three shared filter uniforms (color, filterMatrix, filterMatrixInverse) in each filter's constructor
verdict.helper: a shared base class (e.g. FilterBase extends PIXI.Filter) whose constructor initializes these uniforms, replacing extraction of just these 3 lines
verdict.notes: The three constructors share far more than these 3 lines — they identically set _lastTime, zOrder, animated, and call setTMParams/normalizeTMParams, differing only in the fragment shader and _timeSpeed default. Extracting only the 3-line snippet as a standalone helper is low value; the real win is a base class that consolidates the entire shared constructor body. That makes this a 'maybe' rather than a clear 'factor': the snippet is genuinely duplicated, but the right fix is broader than what the cluster flags.

verdict.what: Identical GLSL `hash2(vec2)` function body duplicated verbatim in four fragment shader strings
verdict.helper: HASH2_GLSL (and companion HASH1_GLSL) — exported string constants interpolated into each shader template literal
verdict.notes: All four files already `import { customVertex2D, applyCustomFilter } from '../filter-core.js'`, so adding `export const HASH2_GLSL` and `export const HASH1_GLSL` there (hash1 is also byte-for-byte identical across all four) and replacing the inline GLSL definitions with `${HASH2_GLSL}` / `${HASH1_GLSL}` inside the template literals is a minimal, zero-risk change. GLSL has no module system so JS-level string interpolation is the correct mechanism. The hash constants differ between hash1 and hash2 — they are not the same function — so keep them as two separate exported constants.

verdict.what: bearing setter that stores degrees, converts to radians, and writes sin/cos components into this.uniforms.dirV
verdict.helper: BearingMixin(Base) — a mixin class providing get/set bearing with the deg→rad→dirV logic
verdict.notes: All three setters are byte-for-byte identical including the getter. All three classes extend PIXI.Filter directly with no shared base, so a mixin (BearingMixin(PIXI.Filter)) is the cleanest vehicle — it keeps the property on the instance, avoids exposing _bearing to a free function, and lets each class declaration simply swap `extends PIXI.Filter` for `extends BearingMixin(PIXI.Filter)`. Medium effort because the mixin pattern must be introduced and imports updated in three files, but the logic change per file is minimal.

verdict.what: object literal fragment with three trigger/activation properties
